newsitem.title: USA: Teamsters, supporters rally against UPS.
newsitem.headline: Teamsters, supporters rally against UPS.

text.p: Striking Teamsters and supporters gathered at an enthusiastic rally Wednesday in a show of strength in their 10-day-old walkout against the United Parcel Service.

Union members drove huge semi-trailers to the rally on the banks of New York Harbor, where pickets held signs reading "Part-time America won't work!" and sang "We'll stay out on the line 'til we get that contract signed."

Speaking with the dramatic backdrop of the Statue of Liberty in the distance, Teamster official George Cashman said of the strike: "It's about people coming to this country and being able to earn a good wage."
"It's as basic as baseball and apple pie," he said.

A third round of talks to end the strike by 184,000 Teamsters against the giant package delivery company was scheduled for Thursday, but Teamsters President Ron Carey said late Wednesday he saw no reason for optimism.
Among the key issues in the dispute are better pay and the Teamsters' demand that UPS convert part-time jobs into full-time jobs. UPS has said it will not improve its latest contract offer.
"It's not a strike for money. It's a strike for what's right," said Teamster Pete Karcich, who works for UPS in Secaucus, N.J., and said he was prepared to survive an extended walk-out.
"Most of us have mortages, kids and big bills," he said. "This is nothing new."
On Tuesday, the AFL-CIO offered millions of dollars to help the striking Teamsters. The money would go toward strike benefits of $55 a week, the labor federation said.
Teamster Roderick Clancy, who attended the rally, said he was opposed to the strike benefits.
"I don't care if it's $55 or $155, because the company sits back and thinks, 'How long can the union last on this kind of money?'" he said.
Cashman, the president of a Teamster local in Boston and a member of the team negotiating with UPS, said less than 1 percent of union members have crossed the picket line.
The picture of a huge rat adorned the side of one of the Teamsters' big trucks, with a warning "Don't be a rat scab."
UPS officials have said they want the union to permit a vote on its last offer, but Carey has insisted his union members have already voted.
Teamster Cathie Cunningham, a part-time UPS worker, said she was angry at the suggestion by UPS.
"It infuriates me," she said, clenching her fists. "Ninety-five percent of us nationwide (already) told Ron Carey you go to Washington and you negotiate for us."
Added Clancy: "You have to trust in the people who are negotiating the contract. You can't second-guess.
"I will go under the assumption of whatever Ron Carey says," he added.
